opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's been a really important part of the story for us. The original motivation for TPUs, back around 2013, was actually a serving problem. We did a back-of-the-envelope calculation: if a lot of people started using speech recognition for even a few minutes a day, and we ran those neural nets on the CPUs we had, we'd need to roughly double the number of computers Google had. That made it clear we needed specialized hardware for inference. The first-generation TPU was an inference chip.

Since then, the big advantage has been co-design. Because the hardware, compiler, and model teams all sit close together, we can look at where the models are heading, things like larger context windows, mixture-of-experts architectures, and lower-precision arithmetic, and make sure the chips and interconnect are built for that. For serving, a lot of it comes down to memory bandwidth and how efficiently you can move weights and KV cache around. The high-bandwidth interconnect between chips in a pod lets you shard a very large model across many chips and still get good latency.

Then there's the software side. Things like quantization, speculative decoding, and distillation into smaller, faster models all compound with the hardware gains. When you multiply those factors together, the cost per token for a given capability level has dropped dramatically over the last few years. That's what lets us put very capable models into products that serve hundreds of millions or billions of people, rather than keeping them as expensive research artifacts.

Looking forward, I think inference will become an even larger share of total compute, especially as models do more reasoning at test time and spend more tokens thinking before they answer. So we're increasingly designing with serving efficiency as a first-class goal, not just training throughput.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The honest answer is that the hardware and the models have been co-designed for a long time now, and that's the whole point. When we started the first TPU back around 2013, the motivation was pretty simple: we did some back-of-the-envelope math and realized that if people started using voice search for a few minutes a day, we'd need to double the number of data centers Google had just to serve the speech models on CPUs. That was obviously not going to work, so we built a chip that was good at one thing, which is dense low-precision linear algebra.

What's changed since then is that serving has become at least as important as training, and in some ways harder. Training is one giant job you can plan for. Serving is millions of requests arriving at unpredictable times, with latency targets measured in tens of milliseconds, and every token you generate on a decoder model is a separate step where you're mostly memory-bandwidth bound rather than compute bound. So the design questions for inference are really about memory: how much high-bandwidth memory is on the chip, how fast can you stream weights and KV cache through it, and how do you move activations between chips without the interconnect becoming the bottleneck.

That's why the interconnect matters so much to us. With the ICI links and the optical circuit switching in the newer generations, we can carve a pod into slices of whatever shape a given model wants. A really large model can be sharded across many chips so its weights fit in collective HBM, and a smaller model can run on a handful of chips at very high throughput. The same physical hardware can be reconfigured depending on the serving mix that day, which is a big operational win.

The other thing I'd emphasize is that we get to use the hardware as a design constraint for the models themselves. Things like mixture-of-experts, speculative decoding, distillation into smaller models, quantization to int8 or lower, all of those are techniques where the payoff depends heavily on what the chip is good at. When your model team and your chip team sit near each other, you can say "the next generation will have this much bandwidth and this sparsity support," and the model architecture adapts to that, and then the chip after that adapts to where the models are going. That feedback loop over several generations is really the capability. It's not any single chip.

And then there's cost. The models people want are getting more capable, but if you can't serve them at a price that lets billions of people use them, they stay demos. Specialized hardware, plus software like XLA and Pathways that can keep it busy across a whole fleet, is what makes the economics work. I think of it less as "TPUs let us serve big models" and more as "TPUs let us keep pushing model quality up while keeping the cost per query from going up with it."

astra-6.text:
I think the key is that you have to design the hardware and the models together. Serving a large model isn’t just about how many arithmetic operations you can do per second. It’s also about how quickly you can move the weights and intermediate results through memory, and how efficiently you can communicate across chips.

TPUs give us a way to optimize that whole system. If you can make inference more efficient, you can serve more requests with the same amount of compute, or spend more computation on each request to improve the quality of the answer.

And latency matters a lot. Throughput is important when you’re serving lots of users, but each user wants a responsive experience. So the interesting challenge is getting the hardware, the model, and the serving software to work together to deliver both.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key is designing the hardware and the models together. Serving a large model isn’t just about how many arithmetic operations you can do. You also have to move the weights and intermediate results around efficiently, and coordinate computation across a lot of chips. Memory bandwidth and the interconnect matter enormously.

TPUs give us a way to optimize that whole system. And at scale, efficiency translates directly into what you can offer users: lower latency, lower cost, or a more capable model within the same serving budget. The interesting challenge is balancing those things, because a system that’s very efficient with large batches may not give you the responsiveness you want for an interactive conversation.
